readings: Hold true to what you have attained
Jesus, the Resurrection and the Life
2027-05-24.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe). Pentecost opened the seven weeks of this season, which recalls the birth of the Church and the mission of the apostles. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angelus (“The Angel of the Lord”) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The second week of the Season of the Apostles begins, the day after the feast of the Most Holy Trinity.
2027-05-24.verse: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live,”
theo: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison, and he writes as a father: “Only let us hold fast to what we have attained. Brothers and sisters, join in imitating me, and observe those who live according to the example you have in us.” It may sound bold to say ‘imitate me’, but Paul has just told them that he himself is still running, pressing on towards the goal (Philippians 3:12–14). He does not offer himself as a finished saint, but as a runner who has not stopped. Faith is passed on this way, from life to life. Every one of us learned to pray from someone: a mother at the evening prayer, a grandfather with his rosary, a catechism teacher, a priest. The Season of the Apostles reminds us that the Church was built on witnesses whose lives could be copied. The question for us is simple: if someone younger imitated my faith, would they come closer to Christ?

Then Paul's voice breaks: “For many live as enemies of the cross of Christ; I have often told you of them, and now I tell you even with tears.” He describes them without hatred, with grief: “Their end is destruction; their god is the belly; and their glory is in their shame; their minds are set on earthly things.” These seem to be not pagans far away but baptized people who have made comfort and appetite their god. The danger is close to every one of us. Against it Paul sets one of the most beautiful lines of the New Testament: “But our citizenship is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.” Philippi was a Roman colony, proud of its citizenship; Paul tells them they belong to a greater city. And the Saviour we await “will transform the body of our humiliation that it may be conformed to the body of his glory.” Our bodies, weak and ageing, are not prisons to escape but seeds of the resurrection. The Catechism quotes these words when it teaches how we will rise: Christ will change our lowly body to be like his glorious body (CCC 999).

The Gospel shows that hope at the graveside. Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha goes out to meet Jesus and speaks with the honesty of grief: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask of him.” Jesus says, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha answers with the faith of a devout Jewish woman of her time: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.” And Jesus brings the last day into the present: “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” Resurrection is not only an event at the end; it is a Person standing before her. Martha's answer is one of the great confessions of the Gospel: “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.” In the Season of the Apostles, when the Church goes out to proclaim the Risen Lord, Martha teaches us the heart of that proclamation. Every Christian funeral in our parishes, with its prayers and its incense and its candles, repeats her words. And every time we visit a grieving family, we bring the same Lord to the door, asking quietly: “Do you believe this?”
conn: Just before today's passage Paul says, “I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:14).
Hebrews says of the patriarchs that “they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16).
Paul to Corinth: “It is sown a physical body, it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44).
Ezekiel 37:12: “I am going to open your graves, and bring you up from your graves, O my people.”
Peter confesses, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16); Martha says the same at Bethany (John 11:27).
In Luke 10:38–42 Martha is busy serving; here she is the first to run out to meet Jesus.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we receive the Body of the One who is the Resurrection and the Life: he gives us the pledge that our lowly bodies will be made like his glorious body.
The Qurbana is the meeting point of our two citizenships: on earth we gather at the altar, and the altar opens onto heaven, where our citizenship is.

Name one person who has drifted from the Church and pray for them with Paul's tears.
Before you make a purchase or a choice this week, ask: does this suit a citizen of heaven?
Go, like Martha, to meet the Lord in a house of mourning: visit or call someone who has lost a loved one.
fathers: Christians live in their own countries, but as sojourners; they share in everything as citizens and endure everything as strangers. Every foreign land is their homeland, and every homeland a foreign land. They pass their days on earth, but they are citizens of heaven.

Martha said, I know that he will rise on the last day. The Lord answered, I am the resurrection: as if to say, you speak of a day that is far off; but the One who will raise him then is here now, and whoever believes in him already passes from death to life.
magis: Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: I am the resurrection and the life.
How do the dead rise? Christ is raised with his own body; he will change our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).
Christ will raise us up on the last day, but it is also true that in a certain way we have already risen with Christ through Baptism.
The Father's house is our homeland; we are citizens of heaven, while we are still on our way.
saints: Second Monday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar a weekday of Ordinary Time (Eighth Week).

23–29 May: second week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 23: the Most Holy Trinity. Tue 25: in the Latin calendar, St Bede the Venerable, St Gregory VII and St Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi. Wed 26: in the Latin calendar, St Philip Neri. Thu 27: the feast of the Body and Blood of Christ, kept by our Church on the Thursday (the Latin Church in India keeps Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May). Sat 29: in the Latin calendar, St Paul VI. Then Sun 30: Third Sunday of the Apostles; Mon 31: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2027-05-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the resurrection and the life. At Bethany you met Martha in her grief and drew from her the confession of faith; meet us also in our sorrows, and make us say with her, Yes, Lord, I believe. Keep us from making our belly our god and setting our minds on earthly things. Remind us that our citizenship is in heaven, and teach us to live so that others may imitate us and come to you. When our bodies grow weak and our days end, transform the body of our humiliation into the likeness of your glorious body, and raise us up to live with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever. Amen.

catechism: Jesus, the resurrection and the life.
kidsaint: Martha was a good friend of Jesus. She lived in Bethany with her sister Mary and her brother Lazarus, and she loved to cook for Jesus when he came to visit. When Lazarus died, Martha ran to meet Jesus, and Jesus told her, ‘I am the resurrection and the life.’ Martha said, ‘Yes, Lord, I believe!’ Then Jesus raised Lazarus from the tomb. The Church remembers her on 29 July.
2027-05-24.special: Second Monday of the Apostles. The day after the feast of the Most Holy Trinity.
term: Paul's image for the Christian's true belonging: as Philippi was a Roman colony whose people were citizens of Rome, so Christians live on earth as citizens of the kingdom of heaven, awaiting the Saviour and the resurrection of the body.

family.explain: Martha's brother Lazarus had died, and she was very sad. When Jesus came, she ran to meet him. Jesus told her, ‘I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live.’ Martha said, ‘Yes, Lord, I believe!’ Jesus is stronger than death. When someone we love dies, we can be sad, but we also have hope: Jesus will raise them up.
family.intention: We pray for our grandparents and relatives who have died, and for families who are sad today.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom do we miss who has gone to God? Let us say a prayer for them now.”

illus: On the anniversary of her husband's death, an elderly widow in Kottayam walks every year to the parish cemetery with her grandchildren. She lights a small oil lamp on the grave, sprinkles holy water and prays aloud the words of Martha. One year her teenage grandson asked why she did not cry anymore. She said, ‘For the first years I cried at this grave. Now I come here to say I believe. Your appachan is not in this stone; he is with the One who said, I am the resurrection. I come to tell him I am still on the way.’ The boy said later that it was the first time he understood what Christians mean by hope.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, resurrection and life, you met Martha on the road in her grief. Meet us now, and strengthen our faith in you. Amen.
share: Join in imitating me, and observe those who live according to the example you have in us (Philippians 3:17). Whose faith has shaped mine, and whom am I shaping?
Our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). What earthly things have too great a hold on my heart?
Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died (John 11:21). What grief or disappointment do I need to bring honestly to Jesus?
I am the resurrection and the life… Do you believe this? (John 11:25–26). How would I answer Jesus today?
pm.resp: Lord, you are the resurrection and the life.
interc: For all who mourn, that the Risen Lord may meet them on the road as he met Martha.
For our beloved dead, that they may rise to the glory of Christ.
For those who live as enemies of the Cross, that they may be turned back with tears and love.
For parents, godparents and teachers, that their lives may be worth imitating.
For our parishes, that they may be communities of hope in time of death and sorrow.
pm.close: Father, you raised your Son and made him the resurrection and the life of all who believe. Strengthen our faith, comfort the sorrowing, and bring us with all our beloved dead to the glory of your kingdom. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today Paul writes from prison to the Christians of Philippi: “join in imitating me.” He is not boasting. He is a runner still pressing on, and he asks them to run with him.

Then he weeps for those who live as enemies of the Cross, whose god is the belly and whose minds are set on earthly things. And he reminds us: “our citizenship is in heaven.” We belong to God's kingdom, and we wait for the Saviour who will transform our weak bodies to be like his glorious body.

In the Gospel Lazarus has died. Martha runs to meet Jesus and says honestly, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Jesus does not scold her. He says, “Your brother will rise again.”
Martha thinks of the last day, but Jesus says, “I am the resurrection and the life.” The resurrection is not only a future day; it is a Person, and he is here.
Jesus asks her, “Do you believe this?” Martha answers, “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God.”
Today he asks the same question of each of us, especially those who are grieving. Let us answer with Martha, and live as citizens of heaven. Amen.
kids: Children, Martha was sad because her brother Lazarus had died. But Jesus told her, ‘I am the resurrection and the life.’ That means Jesus is stronger than death!
When someone we love goes to heaven, we can be sad, but we can also say like Martha: ‘Yes, Lord, I believe!’
